title: Targeted therapy vs. chemotherapy
blurb: Why some drugs hit every dividing cell, and others aim at one broken protein.

text.simple: Classic **chemotherapy** attacks cells that are dividing fast. Cancer cells divide a lot, so they get hit hard. But some healthy cells divide fast too, like hair and the gut lining, which causes side effects.
text.student: Chemotherapy drugs kill fast-dividing cells, mostly by damaging DNA or blocking DNA building blocks. Healthy fast-dividing cells (hair follicles, mouth and gut lining, blood-forming cells) are also hit, causing side effects. [@nci_chemo]
text.deep: Cytotoxic agents (antimetabolites, topoisomerase poisons, DNA crosslinkers, antimitotics) exploit proliferation rate and DNA-damage-response defects; therapeutic index is limited by proliferating normal tissues. [@nci_chemo]

steps.title: Try it: a classic chemo drug

try.note: Methotrexate blocks DHFR, which cells need to make DNA building blocks. Compare the two cells.

text.simple: Methotrexate has been used since the 1950s. It blocks a protein every dividing cell needs.
text.student: Methotrexate targets **DHFR**, an enzyme every dividing cell uses, cancer or not.
text.deep: DHFR knockdown is a weak stand-in for methotrexate's acute nucleotide depletion; the measured knockdown effects are modest.

steps.title: Targeted therapy: aim at the broken part

text.simple: **Targeted drugs** are designed to hit a protein that's broken in the cancer. Imatinib, for example, blocks BCR-ABL1, which only the leukemia cells have.
text.student: Targeted therapies act on specific molecules that drive a cancer. [@nci_targeted] Imatinib transformed chronic myeloid leukemia treatment by blocking BCR-ABL1. [@druker2001]
text.deep: Targeted agents exploit oncogene addiction. Imatinib's clinical success in CML established kinase inhibition as a paradigm, though most targeted drugs still have on- and off-target toxicities. [@druker2001]

try.note: CDK6 knockdown (palbociclib's target) changes the cancer cell's division program but leaves the healthy-like cell almost untouched. Now try MTOR in the playground: it hits both.

text.simple: A good target matters a lot to the cancer cell and very little to healthy cells.
text.student: Compare how much each cell changes. This gap is what drug makers call a **therapeutic window**.
text.deep: Differential dependency between tumor and normal cells defines the therapeutic window; genetic screens across many lines are used to find such selective dependencies.

steps.title: Targeted doesn't mean no side effects

text.simple: Even targeted drugs can cause side effects, because healthy cells often use the same protein a bit too.
text.student: Targeted therapies can still cause side effects, such as skin, gut or liver problems, because normal cells may use the target too, or the drug may hit other proteins. [@nci_targeted]
text.deep: On-target/off-tumor effects (e.g., EGFR inhibitor rash) and off-target kinase inhibition are common sources of toxicity. [@nci_targeted]

quiz.q: Why does chemotherapy often cause hair loss?
options: Hair-follicle cells divide fast, like cancer cells
quiz.explain: Chemo hits fast-dividing cells, including healthy ones in hair follicles. [@nci_chemo]

options: It is injected directly into the tumor
It is designed to act on a specific molecule that drives the cancer
quiz.explain: Targeted therapies act on specific molecules involved in cancer growth. [@nci_targeted]
